summary: Chinese yam, also called cinnamon vine, is a fast-growing vine that climbs over nearby plants and smothers them under a thick layer of leaves, blocking out their sunlight. On trees, the vine can become so heavy that it bends and breaks small branches. In North America, Chinese yam spreads mainly through small bulb-like buds that form along the vine rather than through seeds, and even damaged bulbils can sprout into new plants. Water can transport these bulbils more than 200 meters away.
history: Chinese yam is native to East Asia, including northern China, Korea, and Japan. It is rarely planted in gardens, but the species can spread when yard waste containing its tubers is thrown out. In New York, Chinese yam has been found in the Lower Hudson region and Long Island.

handling.text: Small, isolated patches can be controlled by digging out the entire underground tuber. Large infestations usually need herbicides and repeat treatments, because the deep tubers store food that lets the vine regrow. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
